title: EvoRouter: Cost-Efficient Multi-Agent Routing via Insight-Guided On-Policy Distillation
summary: Serving web queries at scale with multi-agent systems requires jointly configuring large language models, collaboration modes, agent counts, interaction rounds, and skills. However, the resulting configuration space grows combinatorially, while sparse execution rewards provide limited fine-grained supervision for interdependent planning decisions. We propose EvoRouter, a self-evolving multi-agent routing framework driven by insight-guided on-policy distillation. A dedicated expert periodically synthesizes performance-cost feedback from configuration trajectories across tasks into reusable conditional routing insights about capability requirements, returns from resource scaling, and interactions among configuration choices. A privileged teacher combines these evolving insights with current execution feedback to provide dense token-level supervision for the router's own planning trajectories through on-policy distillation. Cost-aware reinforcement learning jointly optimizes task performance and computational cost. Together, these training signals internalize execution insights into the routing policy. The updated policy generates new trajectories that support subsequent insight extraction, forming an execution-driven self-improvement loop. We evaluate EvoRouter on 19 in-domain datasets spanning five domains and two out-of-domain benchmarks. EvoRouter achieves an average in-domain accuracy of 68.69%, outperforming the strongest routing baseline by 7.23 percentage points while reducing inference compute cost by 50.95%. Our code is open-sourced at https://github.com/CenYangtze/EvoRouter.

title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
summary: Root cause analysis (RCA) of microservice failures has attracted many LLM agents whose investigation is hand-crafted, through standard operating procedures, fixed stages and role agents. Each is evaluated on its own data against few baselines, so it is unknown whether this design beats letting a capable model investigate on its own. We compare three simple harnesses that prescribe none of the model's calls (one call over an evidence package, a SQL agent and the Codex coding agent) with five published LLM RCA agents and with statistical and causal methods on RCAtlas, 90 validated cases from eight public datasets, across six models and three reasoning efforts. The simple harnesses are the most accurate (PR@1 65-77% on three mid-tier models), ahead of the published agents (16-53%) and the non-LLM methods (6-39%), on every model on which both families were run. The published agents fix from a tenth to all of their model calls in the program, and a case study shows how these prescriptions skip the decisive evidence. A stronger model mainly improves reliability, a multi-turn harness mainly improves aptitude, and more reasoning effort changes accuracy by a few points at most while multiplying the time by up to seven. Among runs more accurate than the best non-LLM method, every Pareto-optimal run in cost or time uses a simple harness.

title: EvolveMAS: A Unified Self-Evolution Framework for Decentralized Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Decentralized multi-agent systems (MAS) enable large language model agents to interact without centralized control. Agents need to adapt to other agents at test time and reuse accumulated experience to refine their interaction strategies for future interactions across cooperative, mixed-motive, and adversarial settings. However, existing approaches often develop adaptation mechanisms for particular interaction settings. This raises a central question: how can decentralized MAS support test-time adaptation and reliable experience reuse across interaction settings? We propose EvolveMAS, a unified self-evolution framework that supports experience-driven adaptation within and across episodes. EvolveMAS pairs each main agent with a dedicated MemoryAgent for test-time memory governance, which maintains isolated Structured Memory outside the main agent's reasoning context. EvolveMAS organizes adaptation into two complementary processes: Within-Episode Online Adaptation and Cross-Episode Knowledge Evolution. During Within-Episode Online Adaptation, MemoryAgent updates episodic, semantic, and working memory from interaction evidence to inform subsequent actions. During Cross-Episode Knowledge Evolution, the main agent uses memory and episode outcomes to distill reusable interaction knowledge comprising partner profiles and interaction strategies for subsequent episodes. Across five benchmarks and six evaluation configurations spanning the three interaction settings, EvolveMAS achieves the highest normalized average score of 77.2 among the compared methods. Ablations show that test-time memory governance and cross-episode knowledge reuse both improve performance. Interaction traces further illustrate how updated memory and distilled knowledge guide subsequent interactions. These results support experience-driven adaptation in decentralized MAS without updating model parameters.

title: GLM-5.3 Optimizations, Part 2: PCP, DCP, and Hybrid HiSparse on 16 H200s
summary: vLLM serves GLM-5.3 on 16 H200s with PCP and DCP prefill and Hybrid HiSparse decode, reaching 1M-token contexts and 1.7–3.2× the per-user speed of data-parallel P/D on the AgentX agentic benchmark.
story_key: model:glm|ver:5.3|title:glm 5 3 optimizations part 2 pcp dcp and hybrid hisparse on 16 h200s
content_excerpt: TL;DR: Long agentic contexts push GLM-5.3 against two limits on H200s: KV cache memory and prefill speed. We address both on 16 H200s, split into one prefill node and one decode node: Agentic workloads have long contexts that grow with every turn, which puts pressure on both GPU memory and prefill. On H200s, GLM-5.3's weights take up most of each GPU's memory, leaving little room for the KV cache of those long contexts. And because every turn adds more tool output and file contents to prefill, under load the prefill engines can become the bottleneck for the whole deployment. Part 1 showed how Hybrid HiSparse lets long contexts fit in an aggregated deployment on a single 8× H200 node. Prefill/decode disaggregation takes more than that. On the prefill node, we use PCP to speed up long prompts by parallelizing across the prompt's tokens. With MLA, however, this leaves every PCP rank holding a full copy of the KV cache, so we combine it with DCP to remove that replication. On the decode node, Hybrid HiSparse allows higher concurrency at long contexts. vLLM's new modular core ( Model Runner V2 ) makes composing all of this much easier. Neither scheme spreads one long prompt's attention work across the eight GPUs without also keeping its whole KV on each GPU that serves it. The next two sections address each half. PCP splits a prompt's queries across GPUs, and DCP splits its KV. In our 8× H200 prefill engine, PCP splits each prompt across the eight GPUs by token: every GPU computes the queries for one eighth of the prompt, with all 64 heads. A naive split would be unbalanced. Under causal attention a token attends to every token before it, so the GPU holding the end of the prompt would do far more work than the one holding the start. PCP instead cuts the prompt into 16 chunks and pairs them up: GPU takes chunk from the front and chunk from the back, so every GPU gets the same mix of cheap and expensive tokens (Figure 3 shows this as a V-shaped pattern across the eight GPUs). This is the load-balanced sharding from Context Parallelism for Scalable Million-Token Inference . Finally, each GPU's new KV is all-gathered, so every query can still attend to the full context. Figure 1 compares the two splits. PCP fixes both problems. Each GPU indexes only its own tokens, so the indexer is no longer replicated on every GPU and each GPU does an eighth of it. And each KV row read from memory now serves all 64 heads instead of 8, raising sparse MLA from about 26 to about 191

title: Context Engineering (Agent Memory) for AI Agents Starts with Retrieval
summary: Agents waste time and context on clumsy searches, oversized results and stale data. Learn the retrieval techniques LangChain's Deep Agents harness uses to get the right context in.
story_key: story|title:context engineering agent memory for ai agents starts with retrieval
content_excerpt: Imagine you’re taking an open book exam: you technically have all the answers, but somehow that makes it even harder to find the right one. Hand an agent a question and it’s left with a similar predicament: it has a limited context window, so like us humans, it has to retrieve information to complete certain tasks (instead of having everything memorized). When searching, agents struggle with: Luckily, there are several techniques at an agent’s disposal that allow it to retrieve the correct information. It’s the job of an agent harness to apply these techniques strategically to get the model the right context at the right time for the given task. This blog covers the challenges with agent retrieval (finding and pulling in only the information necessary for the task at hand), the techniques at our disposal to combat them, and how to keep these in mind when designing an agent harness (using LangChain’s Deep Agents harness as an example). For more on how to manage context once it's in the context window, check out this blog on Context Engineering . Let’s see how this can be applied in a real-world use case: a competitive analysis agent. Every Monday, an agent researches hundreds of competitors and writes a report in the team's template. It needs to: Each of these is a different kind of retrieval and therefore faces different problems. We've built our agent using the Deep Agents harness so there are a few techniques that we can apply out of the box to minimize these problems. Our agent has to find three things for each competitor. If each one takes a dozen tries (opening files just to see what's inside, or rewording a search because the source uses different words), its context window fills up with failed searches before it even writes a word of the report. Therefore, the best search is the one the agent doesn't have to repeat, and that means using the right tool for each job. One of the most common ways for an agent to search through information is with a filesystem. However, if our agent opens every file to see what's inside, it's searching very inefficiently: each file it reads lands in its context window, so it can fill up just from looking. A better approach is to check names and keywords first (the way you'd scan a book's index instead of reading every page during an open-book exam). title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
summary:
A vulnerability costs more to fix the later it is discovered. As coding agents generate code faster than developers can review it, software needs a first line of defense screening each new function in real time. LLM agents have recently become capable of finding real-world vulnerabilities by working as a security expert would: they run analysis tools, explore the surrounding code, test hypotheses and weigh the evidence before forming their own judgement. This reasoning, however, spans many model calls, so that each verdict takes minutes of compute, far too long for real-time screening. Faster detectors, which fine-tune deep learning models or prompt an LLM for a direct verdict, are less accurate: they judge a function without the context an agent gathers, and an LLM's generated verdict is unreliable even when given some of it.
  We present REVA (REal-time Vulnerability Analysis), an AI vulnerability detector that brings the security context and code understanding components behind agentic detectors into a single forward pass of an LLM. For each new function, REVA gives the LLM a pre-computed threat model of its module, lightweight static analysis findings and call-graph information. REVA leverages a trained probe to read the LLM's internal representations of the new function in this context. On PrimeVul's held-out test set, REVA on GLM-5.3-Flash reaches 60.0% accuracy in about one second per function. This matches VulTriage (59.2%), the state-of-the-art agentic detector, run on the same LLM, while being over 250 times faster and less than a tenth as costly. On the same prompt, the probe is 14% to 17% more accurate than the LLM's own direct verdict. Across three open LLMs, REVA is at least as accurate as VulTriage, and about 10% more accurate on two of them. An LLM's internal representations thus encode much of what agentic detectors obtain through reasoning.

title: FOCUS: Active Critic Learning for Long-Horizon Language Model Agents
summary: Sparse outcome rewards make it difficult for long-horizon language-model agents to assign credit to earlier actions. Learned critics provide value estimates for intermediate states, but these estimates can be inaccurate, while estimating intermediate values with repetitive continuation samples from points within a trajectory incurs substantial costs. To mitigate these issues, we introduce FOCUS, an RL method that uses selective branching to help the critic network learn its value estimator. The rollout controller facilitates active learning for the critic by sampling continuations from states that are expected to most reduce the critic's estimation error. These refined value estimates then score the segment between consecutive states with a TD($λ$) advantage, while the sampled evidence supplies training targets for the critic. FOCUS supports long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning through a modular context-management interface that decouples context management from rollout allocation. Our experiments show that using compaction-induced segment boundaries for value estimation and credit assignment, FOCUS outperforms GRPO and VinePPO with matched per-step generation budgets on legal reasoning, deep search, and code localization benchmarks, improving held-out accuracy at Qwen3.5-9B scale by 7.2 points over the strongest baseline on BrowseComp-Plus (55.4 vs. 48.2) and by 4.1 points on DeonticBench (56.5 vs. 52.4).

summary:
What's changed

  • Added the Monitor tool and plugin monitors on Bedrock, Vertex, and Foundry, and when telemetry or nonessential traffic is disabled; long foreground sleeps are now blocked there too
  • Fixed requests failing behind some gateways and compatible servers that reject the effort-2025-11-24 beta value or mid-conversation system messages; Claude Code now retries without them
  • Fixed background cleanup deleting some recent files, such as pasted images, when cleanupPeriodDays is set to a very large value
  • Fixed compaction after a "Prompt is too long" error keeping too much of a conversation with dense text, such as base64 or SVG, so the next request could fail again
  • Fixed file read permission prompts not showing where a symbolic link leads
  • Fixed a question's auto-continue timeout firing the moment the external editor closed after a long edit
  • Windows: Fixed PreToolUse and PermissionRequest hooks letting a tool call through when Git Bash is missing and the hook's command is only quoted strings, such as a quoted path
  • Improved auto mode's prompt before the first read outside the working directories: it now says when blocking those reads makes shell commands ask for permission
  • Improved memory use of non-interactive sessions (-p, Agent SDK) during compaction when the transcript file is very large
  • Improved a mod's Image to draw inside tmux with allow-passthrough and focus-events on, in kitty, Ghostty, and iTerm2 3.5+ with fullscreen rendering, where it showed only its alt text
  • Linux: Improved /sandbox and the sandbox startup warning to name Ubuntu's AppArmor restriction on user namespaces, and how to lift it, when it keeps bubblewrap from starting the sandbox
  • Changed the error for an MCP tool call that times out in a non-interactive session while the server's elicitation is unanswered: it now tells Claude that no answer came and not to repeat the call
  • [VSCode] Fixed pressing Enter on the plan review card's "Send feedback and keep planning" button approving the plan instead of sending your comments back
  • [VSCode] Fixed the panel showing "Something went wrong" after "Switch branch & continue" on a cloud session opened from Session history's Web tab
  • [Cloud sessions] Added Claude Code cloud sessions and Remote Control permissions to Enterprise custom roles, so Owners can control access to each by role
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a Choose file button to load a cloud environment's setup script from a file
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed failed saves and archives in the cloud environment edit dialog showing no error inside the dialog
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed failed routine API token actions showing only a toast; the error now appears in the routine edit dialog
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved the session start checklist to show a cloud environment's setup script output in a scrolling box
  • [Cloud sessions] Changed turning on Cloud sessions or Remote Control in admin settings to ask for confirmation and list the custom roles that have that permission
  • [Cloud sessions] Changed the cloud environment dialog to open network access, setup script and environment variables from rows instead of listing every editor at once
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude Tag treating ! commands such as !restart and !help as ordinary messages when sent in bold, italic or strikethrough
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude Tag admin channel and workspace pages being replaced by a load error when a background refresh of the bundle list fails
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude Tag's spend limits page in admin settings reporting that no channels match a filter while channel names are still loading
  • [Code Review] Fixed the Code Review admin section hiding its repositories and switches after a failed refresh of the repository list
  • [Code Review] Improved the Code Review admin section to retry the first load and show one Try again banner when it still fails
